title: FinEdge - Redwood Optimize walkthrough (batching & KV cache)
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV cache, with cost model examples tailored to FinEdge payment fraud scoring workload. Discussed throughput targets, latency SLOs, tradeoffs for dedicated vs hosted, and next steps for benchmark runs and pilot pricing.
topics: cost model examples (per-token impact, GPU utilization)
transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Im Lena from Redwood, with Marco, our solutions engineer. Quick intro?
[00:12] Rachel: Hi Lena, Im Rachel, VP Eng at FinEdge. With me Omar and Linda.
[00:18] Marco: Great. Today we will focus on Optimize recommendations, specifically batching and the prefix/KV cache and how that maps to cost. We know you mentioned fraud scoring, around 120 TPS at peak?
[00:34] Omar: Yeah peak QPS around 100 to 150, typical is 40 to 60, and tail latency needs to be under 200ms 95th.
[00:46] Lena: Awesome, thats helpful. Quick agenda: batching patterns, how KV cache works for prefix reuse across similar requests, cost model examples, and recommended next steps.
[01:05] Marco: For batching, Redwood uses adaptive continuous batching, so small requests can be aggregated on a single GPU pipeline. The knob is batch_delay and max_batch_size, and we have autosuggests in Console. For your profile with frequent short prompts, increasing batch_delay slightly to 8-12ms can reduce token cost 15-25% without blowing tail latency.
[01:36] Omar: When you say token cost, is that runtime GPU tokens or billing tokens from Redwood hosted?
[01:42] Marco: Runtime cost here is GPU computation cost per token. On hosted per-token billing we show equivalence, but for Dedicated you care about utilization and effective cost per token. Example: with batch_delay 8ms and 64 max batch, we see 30% better GPU utilization on small prompt workloads.
[02:05] Linda: How does KV cache differ from prefix caching? We have multi-step context and some repeated prefixes from transaction metadata.
[02:13] Marco: Good question. Prefix caching stores the token embeddings/state for the common prefix across requests; KV cache stores key/value attention caches to skip recomputation. Practically, prefix cache is best when identical or highly similar prefixes are repeated. KV cache shines when users have varying suffixes but shared history that can be reused.
[02:40] Lena: For FinEdge, you said many requests share a customer header and some transaction metadata, so prefix caching will help. We ran a small sim for a payments workload: with 20% prefix reuse, cost per inference dropped ~12% and tail latency improved slightly because reuse avoids recompute.
[02:59] Omar: Are there memory concerns with KV cache, like per-session state growth?
[03:05] Marco: Yes, KV cache consumption grows with context length and number of active sessions. We recommend LRU eviction and a session TTL policy. In Dedicated we give you memory tuning and alerts in Console. For example, on A100 80GB a single model with 100k concurrent short sessions could hit memory limits if you keep very long TTLs.
[03:30] Rachel: Ok that sounds like an ops thing. Can we see a cost model that compares hosted per-token pricing vs Dedicated reserved capacity in a 6-month pilot?
[03:39] Lena: We put together a sample cost model in the deck link we shared, but quick high level: if your steady state is 40 QPS with 25 tokens per request and bursts to 120 QPS, hosted is simpler but Dedicated gives 30-50% lower unit cost once you commit. The crossover depends on burst patterns and how much prefix reuse you get.
[04:05] Marco: Specifically, assume 40 QPS steady, 25 tokens = 1M tokens/day. With batching and 20% prefix reuse, effective tokens processed drop by ~18% in compute terms. On Dedicated that flows straight to lower GPU hours; on hosted the per-token price also scales down with volume tiers.
[04:30] Omar: For benchmarks, how do you simulate KV cache hits? We want to reproduce yields.
[04:36] Marco: We provide a benchmark harness that can replay traces and mark prefix matches. I will share the script. For the run we did we replayed 10M requests across a day with 20/80 prefix reuse and measured 95th latency and GPU utilization.
[04:53] Linda: Security wise, if we use prefix caching do we leak PII between tenants? We need strong isolation.
[05:00] Marco: Good point. For Hosted we isolate prefixes per-tenant and encrypted at rest; for Dedicated you get tenant isolation and VPC controls. We also support KMS integration for the cache encryption keys.
[05:15] Rachel: Any compliance docs?
[05:17] Lena: Yes, we will send SOC 2 report, SOC 2 Type II attestation, and the security whitepaper for Dedicated and Private.
[05:25] Omar: Back to tuning, whats the recommended starting config for batch_delay and max_batch_size for our long tail?
[05:31] Marco: Start with batch_delay 6-10ms and max_batch_size 64, observe 95th latency; then tweak batch_delay upwards if latency budget allows. Also enable KV cache for prefixes with hit threshold >10% to get meaningful ROI.
[05:48] Lena: We also recommend a hybrid routing policy: route low-latency critical traffic to a pinned lower-batch instance, and best-effort traffic to a high-throughput pool. That protects your 99th/95th while saving on cost.
[06:05] Rachel: That sounds promising. What about model quantization tradeoffs?
[06:09] Marco: Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput but can degrade quality. For classification/fraud scoring it usually works well; we ran 4-bit quantization for one of our open models and saw negligible AUC drop <0.5% while throughput doubled. We recommend validation on your eval set before production rollout.
[06:30] Omar: How do rollouts work? We want canary then gradual ramp.
[06:34] Lena: Console supports canary, A/B, and automatic rollback based on quality regressions or latency SLO triggers.
[06:41] Marco: Quick demo slide now showing Console Optimize tab, autosuggested batch config, KV cache hit rate visualization, cost delta chart.
[06:52] Lena: Note the cost delta chart shows model cost per 1M effective tokens pre and post optimization.
[07:00] Omar: That chart that assumes X% prefix reuse, is it configurable?
[07:03] Marco: Yes you can plug in your trace metrics or simulate different reuse rates.
[07:10] Rachel: Pricing question: if we run a 3-month pilot on Dedicated with reserved capacity, whats the minimum commit?
[07:16] Lena: Typical pilots start with a monthly minimum equal to one machine equivalent, we can offer a pilot price and scale as you prove the workload. Ill send a tailored proposal.
[07:25] Linda: For audits we need logs of cache access and TTL changes.
[07:29] Marco: Console audit logs include cache operations, key rotation events, and access control changes.
[07:34] Omar: One more technical: when a KV cache hit happens does that bypass token counting for billing?
[07:40] Marco: Billing still counts tokens served for the final response, but compute cost is reduced since we skip some recompute. On-hosted billing is per-response tokens; Dedicated economics reflect lower GPU hours.
[07:54] Rachel: Ok lets move to concrete next steps.
[07:57] Lena: Recap: send security docs and SOC 2, share the benchmark harness and a step-by-step guide for KV cache tests, provide pricing/pilot proposal, and schedule a dedicated benchmarking session.
[08:10] Marco: Ill attach the benchmark script and a sample trace generator.
[08:15] Omar: We can share a sample of our request traces and QPS profile by Thursday.
[08:20] Linda: Ill coordinate with compliance for the SOC review and send questions.
[08:25] Lena: Great. Any other questions?
[08:28] Rachel: No thats it. Thanks both.
[08:31] Lena: Thanks all, we will follow up with the items.
